passage:
Tuesday night. Bad day. The marks came back and I'm sitting on the terrace with a knot in my chest that won't go. Chaitanya once said his brother uses something to "switch off". All evening I've been thinking, what if that's what I need? Just for tonight.
Then I thought: relief that fast probably means I'd want it again tomorrow. That scared me more than the marks did.
So I called Chaitanya instead. He didn't say anything wise, he just stayed on the line while I complained.
Tomorrow I'll go to the football ground before school, and I'm going to ask Ma if I can talk to the school counsellor. It feels small, but it's a start.
Pradeep

qa.q: Where does Pradeep plan to go before school tomorrow?
qa.a: Pradeep plans to go to the football ground.

qa.q: What scared Pradeep more than the marks?
qa.a: Pradeep realised that relief that fast might mean wanting it again the next day, and that scared Pradeep more than the marks did.

qa.q: Which safer coping steps did Pradeep choose?
qa.a: Pradeep called Chaitanya, planned exercise at the football ground, and decided to ask Ma about talking to the school counsellor.

qa.q: What might staying on the line have meant to Pradeep?
qa.a: Chaitanya didn't need wise words; just staying there let Pradeep complain and feel heard, which suggests simple presence can help a friend under stress.

grounding: Shows a teen tempted to use something to ease stress, choosing to talk and try safer coping instead.

passage: Payal, you asked why I still run every morning. When I was fifteen, in the hostel at Kalimpong, my Ama-la fell ill back home and I couldn't go to her. Exams were close and I stopped sleeping. One night a senior left a half bottle of rum in the common room, and I sat staring at it, thinking, just one glass and this weight will lift. My hand was already on it. Then I thought of my uncle, who started drinking 'just for sleep' and ended up needing it for everything. I put it back and knocked on the warden's door instead, crying so hard I couldn't talk at first. She made me tea, sat with me, and took me to the school counsellor the next day. The counsellor suggested running before class. I, Dolma, have been running ever since, and I phone a friend when the weight comes back.

qa.q: What did the senior leave in the common room?
qa.a: A senior left a half bottle of rum there.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling while staring at the rum that night?
qa.a: Dolma felt worn down with worry and sleeplessness and hoped one glass would lift that heavy sadness for a while.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Dolma's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Remembering the uncle who drank 'just for sleep' and knocking on the warden's door; it swapped quick relief for real help.

qa.q: How might the warden have seen Dolma that night?
qa.a: The warden likely saw a frightened, worried student who needed comfort first, so offered tea and then the counsellor.

grounding: An elder's story of wanting alcohol to ease stress, seeing that quick relief can deepen the problem, and turning to a warden, a counsellor and running.

passage: Rain had drummed on the tin roof for three days, the football ground was a lake, and the notice on the counsellor's door said 'On leave till Monday'. Pankaj's board results were due Friday and his chest felt tight all the time. In his uncle's cupboard there was a packet of cigarettes, and he kept thinking about it. Everyone said they calm you down. On Wednesday night he actually took the packet out and stood by the window with it. Then he remembered his uncle coughing every morning, saying he had only started because of exams. Pankaj put it back and knocked on his sister's door. Bidisha pulled out an earphone. 'Can't sleep?' He told her everything. She didn't laugh. She handed him one earbud, played the tabla recordings he used to practise to, and said, 'Tomorrow we go to Ma together, and Monday to the counsellor.' He slept properly for the first time that week.

qa.q: What did the notice on the counsellor's door say?
What was Pankaj feeling as he stood by the window with the packet?
qa.a: He was tense and anxious about his results, tempted by the idea that cigarettes would calm him, and torn about using them.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Pankaj, and why?
qa.a: Talking to Bidisha instead of smoking; she gave him music, company and a plan to see Ma and the counsellor.

qa.q: How does Bidisha see her brother's late-night knock?
qa.a: She sees he is struggling and treats it seriously, offering music and company rather than laughing.

grounding: Shows a teen tempted to use cigarettes to ease stress who instead talks to his sister and turns to music and a counsellor.
